opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, going back to when I was working on this at OpenAI. The objection I hear constantly is: "Well, can't someone just defeat it?" And the honest answer is yes, a sufficiently determined person can. You could ask the model to write in French and then run it through a translator. You could paraphrase it with another, unwatermarked model. You could insert a bunch of emojis and then delete them. I've been very upfront that no watermarking scheme I know of is robust against an adversary who really wants to remove it.

But I think "it can be evaded, therefore it's worthless" is a non sequitur. Almost no security measure survives a determined adversary. Locks can be picked; that doesn't mean we stop putting locks on doors. What matters is how much effort it adds and who you're trying to catch. A huge fraction of misuse is lazy. It's the student who pastes the essay prompt in and turns in whatever comes out. It's the spam operation churning out millions of fake reviews or propaganda posts at scale, where the whole economic logic depends on not doing extra work per item. Raise the cost even a bit, and a lot of that becomes less attractive or detectable.

There's also something nice about the cryptographic approach specifically. The scheme I worked on biases token choices using a pseudorandom function keyed with a secret, so to an ordinary reader the output looks indistinguishable from normal model output; you don't sacrifice quality. Yet anyone holding the key can compute a score over a few hundred tokens and get a statistically strong signal. So you get detection with essentially no cost to the honest user, which is a pretty good trade.

The deeper limitation, I'd say, isn't evasion; it's coordination. Watermarking only helps if the major providers actually deploy it, and there's a real collective action problem: if one company watermarks and its competitor doesn't, users who care about not being detected just switch. And open-weight models can't really be forced to do it at all. So watermarking isn't going to be the solution to AI-generated text. It's one tool in a toolbox that also includes things like classifiers, provenance standards, and just retrieval, where the provider keeps a record of what it generated and you can check against that.

So my view is: it's imperfect, it's evadable, and it's still worth doing, as long as we're honest with people about exactly what it can and can't guarantee.

r001.rationale: The speaker says a user can translate the text to evade the watermark and that they know of no scheme robust against a determined adversary.

r002.rationale: The response argues that watermarking can deter lazy or large-scale misuse by adding effort and cost.

r003.rationale: The response uses locks as an analogy but does not compare watermarking to Google’s efforts to counter search-ranking manipulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so this is the question I get asked more than any other about watermarking, and I think the honest answer is that it depends enormously on what you think the goal is. If the goal is to stop a determined adversary — a nation-state running a disinformation campaign, say — then no, a watermark isn't going to stop them. They can paraphrase the output with a second model, they can translate it into French and back, they can just use an open-weights model that doesn't have a watermark at all. I've never claimed otherwise, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who did.

But I think that framing misses most of the actual use cases. When I was at OpenAI working on this, the thing I kept coming back to was: who are the people we're actually worried about? And a huge fraction of them are not sophisticated adversaries. They're students who have an essay due at midnight. They're people churning out spam reviews or SEO content at scale. They're someone who wants to pass off a chatbot's output as their own with the minimum possible effort. For those people, the question isn't "can this be defeated in principle," it's "how much work does defeating it take, and is that more work than just writing the thing yourself?" If evading the watermark means you have to substantially rewrite the text, well, at some point you've just written an essay, which was sort of the point.

The analogy I like is locks on doors. Every lock can be picked. Nobody concludes from this that locks are worthless. They raise the cost, they filter out the casual case, and they shift the problem from "anyone can walk in" to "you need to actually commit to doing something you know is wrong." There's also a real deterrence effect that comes from the mere existence of the scheme, independent of how often it's actually used to catch anyone.

The scheme I came up with — the one with the pseudorandom function that biases the sampling toward tokens that score high on a secret key — has the nice property that it doesn't degrade the quality of the text at all in expectation, and it's statistically robust to a certain amount of editing. You can change some fraction of the words and still detect it with high confidence, given enough text. Where it gets genuinely hard is paraphrasing with another strong model, and I think there's an open research question there about whether you can design watermarks that survive semantic-preserving transformations. I'm not sure the answer is yes. It might be a fundamental limit.

The other thing I'd say is that the biggest obstacle to watermarking turned out not to be technical at all. It was that no company wants to deploy it unilaterally, because it's a competitive disadvantage — your users don't want to be watermarked, and they'll go to the competitor who doesn't do it. So you end up in a coordination problem that really needs either an industry agreement or regulation to solve. The cryptography was the easy part, and that's been a somewhat frustrating lesson for me.

r001.rationale: The response says translation and paraphrasing can evade a watermark and describes semantic-preserving robustness as an open question, but it does not specifically say the speaker does not know how to make a watermark survive translation between languages.

r002.rationale: It argues that watermarks still help with less sophisticated misuse by making evasion take substantial rewriting effort, potentially more work than writing the text oneself.

r003.rationale: The response uses locks as an analogy and discusses deterrence and coordination, but does not compare watermarking to Google's efforts to combat search-ranking manipulation.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the right question is: useful against whom, and for what purpose? If someone is determined to remove a watermark, and they’re willing to rewrite the text extensively, then yes, they may be able to do that. You shouldn’t present watermarking as an infallible way to identify everything that came from an AI.

But it doesn’t follow that it’s useless. A lock can be picked, and yet we still put locks on doors. A watermark could help identify some AI-generated text, or make it more costly to produce large amounts of text while concealing its origin. Those are more modest goals, but they can still matter.

The crucial thing is to distinguish a positive detection from a negative one. If you find a sufficiently strong watermark, that could be evidence about where the text came from. If you don’t find one, that doesn’t establish that a human wrote it. And you have to be extremely careful about false positives, especially if anyone is going to use the result to accuse someone of misconduct.

So I’d think of it as one tool among several. The fact that there are ways around it is a reason to understand its limitations and test it against attacks, rather than either promise that it solves the whole problem or dismiss it outright.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the right question is not whether a watermark is impossible to remove. If someone is sufficiently determined, and willing to rewrite the text or run it through another model, then yes, they may be able to remove it. The question is whether it’s useful despite that.

You can imagine a watermark that lets you detect that a long passage came from a particular model, with a very low false-positive rate, without noticeably changing the quality of the text. That could be useful even if it doesn’t catch every case. It gives you a signal that you otherwise wouldn’t have.

Now, you have to be honest about the limitations. Failure to detect a watermark doesn’t establish that a human wrote something. And if evading it becomes completely automatic and essentially free, that reduces its value. But the existence of an evasion strategy doesn’t, by itself, settle the question. You want to know how much effort evasion takes, how much it degrades the output, and what fraction of people will actually bother. I’d view watermarking as one tool among several, rather than a complete solution to the problem of provenance.
